title: Ten thousand replies, still wrong?
hook: An open web poll gets 10,000 replies. What do they tell you about the whole town?

knows: bigger random samples give smaller margins (halve-the-margin-cost)
sample size need not grow with the population (city-poll-nation-poll)
doesNotKnow: that when who answers depends on the answer, a bigger sample does not shrink the error

misconception: A poll with 10,000 replies must be closer to the truth than one with 1,000.
objective: The learner can explain that a self-selected poll stays wrong at any size because who replies depends on the answer, while more replies only make it more precise around the wrong value.

claims.text: If opponents reply at twice the rate of backers in a 50/50 town, every batch of replies holds two opponents per backer, so a self-selected poll's expected share of backers is 1/3 (about 33%) at any sample size; more replies only shrink the margin around that wrong value.
claims.source: Backers reply at rate r, opponents at 2r: expected share = 0.5r / (0.5r + 0.5 x 2r) = 1/3, independent of n. Margin 1.96 sqrt(p(1-p)/n): about ±2.9 at 1,000, ±0.9 at 10,000, ±0.3 at 100,000 points. Brief 59 check (company/domains/briefs/checks/probability-round4-check.mjs).

claims.text: The card's seeded web polls show 35.3% (1,000 replies), 32.3% (10,000) and 33.1% (100,000); its 1,000 random calls show 48.7%.
claims.source: Demo.tsx run(): each reply backs the plan if rng() < 1/3 (web) or < 1/2 (calls). Seeds fixed by poll before looking at results, not chosen: web 1,000 mulberry32(591), 10,000 (592), 100,000 (593); calls mulberry32(59), the brief's seed, which the brief's check also gives as 48.7%. Builder's run, Node 22, 2026-10-14.

claims.text: A random sample of 1,000 has a 95% margin of about ±3.1 points for a 50/50 question, so the random calls land near the truth because everyone had the same chance of being asked.
The town, the plan and the reply rates are a model; in the model the random calls reach anyone and everyone called answers.
claims.source: Lesson rule (brief 59 planned claim 4); stage caption 'Web: opponents reply twice as often. Calls: random.'

claims.text: (Not shown to the learner.) Optional context: the 1936 Literary Digest poll as the classic example of a huge but biased sample.
claims.source: Brief 59 planned claim 5. NEEDS A HUMAN SOURCE CHECK. Not in learner text.

recall.question: A restaurant review site has 50,000 reviews; unhappy diners are much more likely to post. Does the huge count make its average rating trustworthy?
options: No, the reviews over-represent unhappy diners however many there are
Only if there are more than 100,000
recall.why: When who answers depends on the answer, more answers repeat the same bias. Size shrinks the noise, not the bias.
